title: Benchmarking environment best practices (Redwood x NVIDIA)
summary: Redwood walked NVIDIA through the Q1 2026 perf baseline plan and asked for concrete guidance to reduce variance across baseline runs (H100/A100/L40S) and across regions. NVIDIA recommended standardizing on a small set of driver/CUDA combos, enabling persistence mode, avoiding mixed workloads on the same host, pinning CPU/NUMA, and using either application clocks or at minimum enforcing consistent power limits and monitoring GPU clocks/temps via DCGM. They also advised a consistent warmup phase and separating “cold” vs “warm cache” scenarios. Call ended with an agreed set of recommended settings and action items for Redwood to incorporate into the perf suite run manifest and benchmark fleet runbooks.
topics: Driver/CUDA version pinning strategy for reproducible perf
Clock locking (application clocks) vs power limit strategy in cloud environments
Host isolation: exclusive GPU access, noisy neighbor avoidance, CPU pinning/NUMA
Thermal and boost behavior: monitoring clocks/temps, warmup, steady-state windows
Instrumentation: DCGM counters, nvidia-smi snapshots, run manifest fields
questions: What is the minimum set of env capture fields NVIDIA recommends for attribution (driver/CUDA, clocks, power, thermals)?
When clock locking is not available (managed cloud), what is the next best control to reduce variance?
Should Redwood disable GPU auto-boost or TF32 for baselines, or keep defaults and only record them?
How to handle H100 MIG or time-slicing if fleet scheduling forces sharing?
action_items: Rina Kobayashi: Add standardized pre-run and post-run nvidia-smi + DCGM capture to the benchmark harness; include outputs in run artifacts (by 2025-12-19).

Sean Gallagher: Update benchmark cluster runbook to require persistence mode, exclusive process mode where possible, and CPU/NUMA pinning; document the exceptions for cloud SKUs that disallow clock locking (by 2025-12-22).
Sana Farid: Define a warmup + steady-state measurement window policy (including how long to warm, and which samples to discard) and incorporate into noise model notes (by 2025-12-23).
Hiro Tanaka: Share Redwood’s current driver/CUDA/Triton matrix and proposed “supported baseline combos” for NVIDIA sanity check (by 2025-12-12).
Alex Chen (NVIDIA): Confirm recommended application clock targets for H100 SXM vs PCIe and A100 (and any gotchas on L40S) and send a short note Redwood can paste into runbook (by 2025-12-15).
next_steps: Redwood to implement environment capture + warmup rules in the perf suite and validate variance improvements on one H100 and one A100 host.
NVIDIA to send recommended command snippets (nvidia-smi / dcgmi) and guidance on what is “safe” in public cloud vs bare metal.
Schedule a follow-up 30 min review after Redwood’s first controlled re-run (target week of 2025-12-16).
recommended_settings: Pin to a small set of known-good driver/CUDA combos per GPU SKU; avoid mixing in the same baseline report.
Enable persistence mode (nvidia-smi -pm 1) on benchmark hosts.
Prefer exclusive access per GPU (no co-tenancy); avoid MIG for baseline unless you baseline MIG explicitly.

If allowed: set application clocks (nvidia-smi -ac <memClock,graphicsClock>) and keep a consistent power limit; if not allowed: at minimum enforce consistent power limit and monitor actual clocks/temps during the run.
Record and alert on deviations: average/low GPU clocks, throttling reasons, power draw, temps, ECC events.
Standardize warmup: run a fixed warmup workload long enough to reach steady thermals, then measure for a fixed time window; discard early samples.
Pin CPU + memory locality (NUMA) and avoid background host noise; keep container/runtime versions fixed and record them in the run manifest.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Benchmarking environment best practices (Redwood x NVIDIA)
Date: 2025-12-10
Start time: 9:00 AM PT
Duration: 56 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees:
- Hiro Tanaka (Redwood Inference)
- Rina Kobayashi (Redwood Inference)
- Sean Gallagher (Redwood Inference)
- Sana Farid (Redwood Inference)
- Omar El-Sayed (Redwood Inference)
- Alex Chen (NVIDIA)
- Priya Nair (NVIDIA)
- Miguel Ortega (NVIDIA)

---

[00:00] Hiro Tanaka: Alright, thanks everyone for joining. This is, uh, a technical deep dive. We’re trying to lock down benchmarking environment best practices for our Q1 baseline runs. Specifically variance. We’re seeing like p99 TTFT jitter that we can’t always attribute.

[00:18] Priya Nair: Yep, thanks Hiro. Happy to help. Alex and Miguel are on, they do a lot of the “why does my benchmark move 7%?” conversations.

[00:26] Alex Chen: Hey all. So just to calibrate: you’re benchmarking LLM inference, like prefill and decode, right? Continuous batching, those things.

[00:33] Rina Kobayashi: Exactly. We have chat streaming, long-context prefill stress, tool calling bursty stuff, embeddings high QPS. We want it reproducible across H100, A100, L40S, and across us-east / eu-west.

[00:48] Sean Gallagher: And we’re trying to make a run manifest that captures enough to explain deltas, without making it… you know, a PhD thesis.

[00:56] Alex Chen: (laughs) Yep. Benchmarking is basically making a thesis out of a bash script.

[01:03] Hiro Tanaka: The concrete questions for NVIDIA: driver/CUDA settings, clock locking, and isolation. We’re also running in containers (k8s on our bench fleet), so there’s cgroup and NUMA stuff.

[01:18] Miguel Ortega: Got it. First thing I’ll say: pick a driver + CUDA combo and don’t move it mid-baseline. It sounds obvious but it’s usually the #1 issue.

[01:27] Sana Farid: When you say combo—do you mean driver version and CUDA runtime in container? Or host driver only.

[01:34] Miguel Ortega: Both matter. Host driver is the hard constraint. But we also see variance when people switch container images with different CUDA minor, cuBLAS, NCCL, that sort of thing.

[01:45] Alex Chen: For inference you’ll also have kernel stacks like Triton or custom kernels. The point is: pin everything, and write it down. Driver build, CUDA runtime version, and any library versions you can.

[02:01] Rina Kobayashi: That’s aligned with our run manifest schema. We capture driver, CUDA, runtime git SHA, and a “kernel selection matrix” version. What we don’t capture today are like actual observed clocks.

[02:14] Alex Chen: Yep, you want observed. nvidia-smi shows you requested and current. Better: DCGM. But start with nvidia-smi snapshots pre and post.

[02:26] Sean Gallagher: What’s the minimal set you’d recommend to capture each run?

[02:31] Alex Chen: Minimum: `nvidia-smi -q` (or a reduced set), plus `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=timestamp,name,uuid,driver_version,pstate,clocks.current.graphics,clocks.current.sm,clocks.current.memory,clocks.current.video,power.draw,power.limit,temperature.gpu,utilization.gpu,utilization.memory` in CSV. And then record throttling reasons.

[02:55] Omar El-Sayed: Is that the “clocks_throttle_reasons” field?

[02:58] Alex Chen: Yeah. Sometimes it’s called “clocks throttle reasons” and it’s like power cap, thermal, reliability, or application clocks. If you see power throttling in the middle of a run, your p99 will go nuts.

[03:16] Hiro Tanaka: Okay. On clock locking: we’ve had mixed guidance. Some teams set application clocks, some set power limit, some do nothing. What’s your recommended practice, and what’s safe in a cloud fleet?

[03:33] Miguel Ortega: If you can do application clocks, do it. That’s the cleanest. Something like `nvidia-smi -ac` for mem and graphics. But cloud providers often restrict it.

[03:45] Sean Gallagher: Right, that’s what we’re seeing. On some managed instances we can’t set `-ac`.

[03:50] Alex Chen: In that case, you can still reduce variance: ensure persistence mode is on, make sure the power limit is stable (and not bouncing), and avoid concurrent jobs on the same host.

[04:03] Rina Kobayashi: Persistence mode meaning `nvidia-smi -pm 1`.

[04:06] Alex Chen: Yep.

[04:08] Sana Farid: Why does persistence mode matter for our measurements? We’re running steady traffic for like 10–15 minutes.

[04:15] Miguel Ortega: It’s mostly about avoiding driver init and clock gating transitions between runs, and it can help with consistency across runs if your harness stops/starts frequently. Also helps avoid the GPU going into low power states between bursts.

[04:33] Omar El-Sayed: We do have bursts in the tool-calling workload, like multi-turn with gaps.

[04:38] Miguel Ortega: Exactly. You can see it in pstate transitions.

[04:46] Hiro Tanaka: What about “locking clocks” with `-lgc`? I’ve seen folks do `nvidia-smi -lgc min,max`.

[04:54] Alex Chen: That’s another way, but again permissions. In general, for baseline: (1) if bare metal, set application clocks, set power cap, log everything; (2) if cloud restricts, do the best you can and measure observed clocks.

[05:12] Sean Gallagher: We can probably have two bench tiers: “strict” on our owned fleet and “best effort” on rented capacity.

[05:18] Priya Nair: That’s pretty common.

[05:22] Rina Kobayashi: Can you speak to H100 specifically? We have both H100 SXM and PCIe depending on vendor. Does the recommendation differ?

[05:31] Miguel Ortega: Yes. The max clocks and the thermal/power envelope differs. So don’t assume the same “target” is correct across form factors.

[05:41] Alex Chen: And that’s why you shouldn’t only write “H100” in the manifest. Write “H100-SXM” vs “H100-PCIe” if possible, or at least the PCI ID plus memory size. `nvidia-smi` will tell you.

[05:57] Sana Farid: That’s good. We’ve had “same GPU SKU” but different host configs driving variance.

[06:05] Sean Gallagher: On host isolation. We run Kubernetes jobs. What are the hard rules to avoid noisy neighbors?

[06:12] Alex Chen: The hard rule: single tenant per GPU. No time-slicing, no MPS sharing, no MIG unless that’s what you’re benchmarking.

[06:22] Sean Gallagher: We can enforce device plugin allocation, yes. But there’s still CPU noise, I/O.

[06:27] Miguel Ortega: Right. Pin CPU for the container. Make sure interrupts aren’t all on the same socket. NUMA locality matters: if your GPU is on socket 0 and your container is scheduled with CPUs on socket 1, you’ll see jitter.

[06:45] Omar El-Sayed: For our runtime, the scheduler thread and networking are CPU sensitive, especially for streaming.

[06:52] Alex Chen: Exactly. Streaming TTFT vs first byte can be influenced by CPU scheduling, not GPU.

[07:00] Hiro Tanaka: We’ve had a debate internally about TTFT definition: first token computed vs first token on wire.

[07:06] Alex Chen: Yeah, define it and stick to it. But for environment stability: if you can, isolate network and CPU so you’re not measuring client overhead.

[07:18] Rina Kobayashi: We’re doing in-cluster load gen close to the server, but not same pod. We try to avoid crossing AZ.

[07:25] Sean Gallagher: Also: we’re thinking to disable CPU frequency scaling, like set performance governor.

[07:30] Miguel Ortega: Yes. That helps. And huge pages can help, but it’s less the GPU side and more the CPU side.

[07:41] Sana Farid: What about ECC? Should we capture ECC errors? We’ve had one host show weirdly lower throughput.

[07:48] Alex Chen: Yes, capture ECC state and any corrected errors. If you have an active issue it can downclock or cause retries. It’s rare but it happens.

[08:01] Hiro Tanaka: Okay. On thermal: do you recommend warmup? We’re adding standardized warmup because of variance.

[08:07] Miguel Ortega: Absolutely. Benchmarks that start cold then measure right away will be noisy. Warm up until temps and clocks stabilize. Then measure steady state.

[08:18] Sana Farid: Any rule of thumb for how long?

[08:21] Miguel Ortega: Depends on workload, but we often say 5 minutes warmup minimum, sometimes 10 for long prefill that saturates memory.

[08:32] Alex Chen: Also: don’t mix warmup and measurement in the same stats. Discard first N requests or first M minutes.

[08:41] Rina Kobayashi: We can implement that. Our harness can discard first X samples.

[08:45] Sean Gallagher: For long-context prefill, our TTFT p99 improves after caches and after the GPU hits a stable state.

[08:52] Alex Chen: Right. But note there are two things: thermal warmup and cache warmup. KV cache “warm” is different. You probably want both scenarios: cold cache and warm cache.

[09:05] Omar El-Sayed: Yeah we decided to report cold and warm. There was a Slack argument about it.

[09:10] Alex Chen: (laughs) Good.

[09:12] Hiro Tanaka: On MIG and MPS: we don’t plan to use MIG for baseline, but the bench fleet sometimes has MIG enabled for other jobs. Should we hard-disable it?

[09:23] Miguel Ortega: Yes. If MIG is enabled it changes scheduling and memory partitioning. You don’t want that if you’re aiming for “full GPU baseline.”

[09:33] Sean Gallagher: So enforce MIG off and verify in preflight.

[09:36] Miguel Ortega: Exactly.

[09:40] Rina Kobayashi: Are there any driver flags or env vars we should standardize for determinism? Like TF32, math mode.

[09:47] Alex Chen: For inference, TF32 can change performance. If your baseline is meant to reflect production defaults, don’t change it—just record it. If you want a “strict math” baseline, that’s a different baseline.

[10:03] Sana Farid: So recommendation is: keep production-like settings, but capture them.

[10:07] Alex Chen: Yes. Otherwise you risk optimizing for a benchmark that doesn’t match what customers see.

[10:16] Hiro Tanaka: That’s consistent with our program. We want production economics and stability.

[10:22] Priya Nair: Can I ask, what’s your variance target? Like what counts as “noise.”

[10:27] Sana Farid: We’re trying to get run-to-run within ~1–2% on throughput and within a few ms on p95 TTFT for stable cohorts. p99 is trickier.

[10:37] Alex Chen: That’s reasonable. p99 will always be more sensitive to OS scheduling and occasional hiccups. Your best bet is increase sample size and have a policy for outlier analysis.

[10:50] Omar El-Sayed: We’re adding instrumentation for queue wait and batch assembly time. That helps explain p99 spikes.

[10:57] Miguel Ortega: Good. And correlate it with GPU telemetry. Sometimes a p99 spike lines up with a power throttle event.

[11:06] Sean Gallagher: For DCGM, do you recommend always-on exporter or just point-in-time?

[11:12] Alex Chen: For benchmarking, point-in-time plus a small time series is good. You don’t need to ship all of Prometheus if it adds noise. But it’s fine if it’s light.

[11:26] Rina Kobayashi: Our bench hosts already run node exporter. We can add dcgm-exporter but we worry about overhead.

[11:33] Miguel Ortega: The overhead is generally small, but if you’re chasing p99 at millisecond-level, it matters. A compromise: run DCGM sampling at 1s or 5s, not 100ms.

[11:47] Sana Farid: Okay.

[11:49] Hiro Tanaka: We also have kernel auto-selection. Sometimes it picks a different kernel depending on sequence length distribution. That changes perf. We’re adding “kernel selection dumps.”

[12:00] Alex Chen: That’s good. Also: make sure your random seeds and request mix are fixed, or at least recorded.

[12:06] Rina Kobayashi: Yep. Workload seed is in the manifest.

[12:10] Alex Chen: Great.

[12:12] Sean Gallagher: One issue: GPU clocks differ across regions. Like eu-west seems consistently lower average clocks. Could be ambient temp or a different host vendor.

[12:23] Miguel Ortega: Could be both. Different data centers have different thermal profiles. Also different BIOS and power configs. That’s why you want to capture as much host metadata as you can.

[12:35] Sean Gallagher: In k8s we don’t always have access to BIOS info.

[12:38] Alex Chen: Then at least capture what you can: GPU model, power limit, temperature, and actual clocks. Those are the main ones.

[12:49] Omar El-Sayed: If we see lower clocks, should we discard those runs?

[12:53] Alex Chen: Not automatically. But you should flag them. You might have a “non-compliant environment” tag. If it’s systematic for a region, that’s valuable info.

[13:06] Sana Farid: That’s a good point: baseline should reflect reality, but also we need stability.

[13:12] Hiro Tanaka: Right. The baseline is not a marketing benchmark; it’s internal gating.

[13:17] Priya Nair: Exactly.

[13:20] Rina Kobayashi: What about L40S? It’s not data center HPC like A100/H100, but we run some workloads there.

[13:28] Miguel Ortega: L40S can be more sensitive to power management and graphics clocks. Again, log clocks and power draw.

[13:37] Alex Chen: Also check you’re not accidentally running display-related drivers or headless config differences. In servers it’s usually fine.

[13:45] Sean Gallagher: We run headless.

[13:47] Alex Chen: Great.

[13:49] Hiro Tanaka: Okay, can we get into concrete “runbook commands” that you recommend for baseline runs?

[13:55] Alex Chen: Sure. For bare metal or where you have privileges:
- `nvidia-smi -pm 1`
- set power limit to a known value (whatever is default for the SKU, or your chosen cap)
- set application clocks if allowed
- verify no MIG: `nvidia-smi -q | grep -i mig` (or the MIG mode line)
- set exclusive process mode if you’re not using MPS (some environments): `nvidia-smi -c EXCLUSIVE_PROCESS`

[14:25] Sean Gallagher: Does exclusive process mode matter if k8s already assigns the device?

[14:29] Miguel Ortega: It’s defense-in-depth. If something else tries to open a context, it’ll fail.

[14:36] Sean Gallagher: Got it.

[14:38] Rina Kobayashi: And for capturing:

[14:40] Alex Chen: Pre-run: query clocks, power, temps, pstate. During run: sample DCGM metrics every second or five seconds. Post-run: query again.

[14:54] Sana Farid: What DCGM fields do you recommend?

[14:57] Miguel Ortega: GPU utilization, SM clocks, memory clocks, power draw, temperature, and the “throttle reasons” if available.

[15:07] Omar El-Sayed: We can also capture PCIe RX/TX maybe.

[15:11] Alex Chen: Yep if you suspect host bottlenecks. But for LLM inference the big ones are clocks/power/temp.

[15:20] Hiro Tanaka: There’s also the question of kernel compilation caches. We use Triton sometimes; first run compiles.

[15:28] Alex Chen: That’s another warmup category. You want to compile ahead or include compile time as a separate measured thing. For perf baseline, compile should not be in the measured window.

[15:40] Rina Kobayashi: We’re adding warmup to address both. First run compiles, then we measure.

[15:46] Alex Chen: Great.

[15:48] Sean Gallagher: Is there anything else that frequently bites people?

[15:52] Miguel Ortega: CPU affinity. People ignore it, then they wonder why TTFT for streaming is noisy. Also: make sure your benchmark job isn’t competing with log shipping or other daemons.

[16:05] Sean Gallagher: We can run a “benchmark node pool” with minimal daemons.

[16:09] Miguel Ortega: Exactly.

[16:11] Sana Farid: For statistical stability: do you recommend multiple repetitions vs one long run?

[16:17] Alex Chen: Both. One long run is good for steady state. Multiple repetitions catches run-to-run environment drift. If you can do 3 repeats of the same workload, you can estimate variance.

[16:32] Rina Kobayashi: That’s in our plan: 3 to 5 replicates.

[16:35] Alex Chen: Great.

[16:38] Hiro Tanaka: Let’s talk about “clock locking in cloud.” If we can’t lock clocks, what’s the best alternative? Power limit is sometimes also restricted.

[16:49] Miguel Ortega: Then your best control is isolation and observability. You can’t control the GPU firmware settings, so you record what happened. And you ensure no co-tenant workloads. Also: run long enough that transient boost differences average out.

[17:06] Sana Farid: So more sample size and longer windows.

[17:09] Miguel Ortega: Yep.

[17:12] Omar El-Sayed: For long-context prefill, we sometimes saturate memory bandwidth. Does that change guidance?

[17:19] Alex Chen: It means thermals matter more, because sustained bandwidth can heat the GPU. So warmup matters.

[17:27] Rina Kobayashi: We saw that: prefill runs start fast and then settle.

[17:31] Alex Chen: Yep.

[17:33] Sean Gallagher: On host-level isolation: do you recommend “one process per GPU” in general?

[17:39] Miguel Ortega: For baseline, yes. For production you might do multiplexing, but baseline should be “clean.”

[17:47] Hiro Tanaka: That matches our intention.

[17:50] Priya Nair: You mentioned competitors earlier—do you compare with vLLM or TensorRT-LLM? Just curious.

[17:56] Hiro Tanaka: Sometimes in internal experiments. But this program is about our own runtime regression detection.

[18:02] Priya Nair: Got it.

[18:04] Rina Kobayashi: Another question: should we disable GPU “auto boost” or any dynamic features?

[18:10] Alex Chen: Generally no, unless you’re doing microbench. For real workload baselines, keep defaults; those features are part of real perf.

[18:21] Sana Farid: Okay.

[18:23] Sean Gallagher: We have one more issue: on some hosts, we see different PCIe generation, like gen3 vs gen4. Might matter for embeddings throughput.

[18:32] Alex Chen: Could matter if you’re transferring a lot. For embeddings, often the payload is small though. But still, record PCIe link width/speed if you can.

[18:44] Sean Gallagher: We can query with nvidia-smi?

[18:47] Miguel Ortega: nvidia-smi has some PCI info; you can also use `lspci` if permitted.

[18:53] Sean Gallagher: Okay.

[18:55] Hiro Tanaka: Let’s shift to “recommended baseline settings” that we can put into our runbook. I’ll read back what I’m hearing and you correct.

[19:03] Hiro Tanaka: 1) Pin driver/CUDA/container/library versions; don’t change mid-baseline.

[19:08] Alex Chen: Yes.

[19:09] Hiro Tanaka: 2) Persistence mode on.

[19:11] Miguel Ortega: Yes.

[19:12] Hiro Tanaka: 3) Prefer application clocks / power limit when possible; otherwise log observed clocks and throttling.

[19:19] Alex Chen: Yes.

[19:21] Hiro Tanaka: 4) No MIG/MPS sharing; one tenant per GPU.

[19:25] Miguel Ortega: Correct.

[19:27] Hiro Tanaka: 5) CPU/NUMA pinning; performance governor; minimize daemons.

[19:32] Alex Chen: Yes.

[19:34] Hiro Tanaka: 6) Warmup: both compilation warmup and thermal warmup; discard early samples.

[19:40] Miguel Ortega: Yes.

[19:42] Hiro Tanaka: 7) Capture pre/during/post telemetry via nvidia-smi or DCGM.

[19:47] Alex Chen: Yep.

[19:49] Rina Kobayashi: One more: record ECC state and errors.

[19:52] Alex Chen: Yep.

[19:54] Sana Farid: And do at least 3 repeats for variance estimate.

[19:58] Miguel Ortega: Correct.

[20:00] Sean Gallagher: Can you also comment on “exclusive process mode”—is that still recommended?

[20:05] Alex Chen: If you can set it, yes. It prevents accidental multi-context use.

[20:11] Sean Gallagher: Okay.

[20:13] Omar El-Sayed: We also have in-runtime instrumentation (queue wait, batch assembly). NVIDIA, anything you’ve seen useful to correlate?

[20:22] Miguel Ortega: Those are great. Also correlate with GPU utilization; if queue wait spikes but GPU utilization drops, you likely have CPU/network bottleneck. If utilization stays high but TTFT spikes, maybe GPU throttling or memory pressure.

[20:41] Omar El-Sayed: Great.

[20:44] Rina Kobayashi: We’ll add those as tags in the run artifacts.

[20:48] Priya Nair: Do you want us to send a short written note with recommended clocks per SKU?

[20:54] Hiro Tanaka: Yes please. If you can give us “for H100 SXM typical app clocks are X/Y” and same for PCIe and A100. Even if it’s “use default max” but be consistent.

[21:08] Alex Chen: We can send guidance. Just a caveat: exact numbers depend on vendor and power limits. But we can give ranges and what to watch.

[21:18] Sana Farid: That’s fine. We mainly want to detect “something is off.”

[21:23] Sean Gallagher: Another operational thing: benchmark fleet permissions. Sometimes engineers can’t run nvidia-smi flags because of IAM.

[21:31] Miguel Ortega: Right. You’ll need admin on the host for clock settings. If you can’t, don’t fight it—log and accept that tier as best-effort.

[21:43] Sean Gallagher: We’ll formalize which runs are “strict baseline” vs “observational.”

[21:49] Hiro Tanaka: Good.

[21:51] Rina Kobayashi: One more question: should we do “clock locking” for L40S? Or it’s different because it’s like… a workstation-ish GPU.

[22:00] Alex Chen: L40S still supports application clocks, but again depends on the environment. The big thing is consistent power/thermals.

[22:09] Rina Kobayashi: Okay.

[22:11] Sana Farid: If we do strict controls, how much variance should we expect still?

[22:17] Miguel Ortega: It depends. But you can get throughput variance down to ~1% if you’re careful. Tail latency variance is harder; aim to bound it with sample size and stable environment.

[22:32] Sana Farid: Great.

[22:34] Hiro Tanaka: We’re at about half time. I want to make sure we end with action items and a recommended settings list.

[22:41] Priya Nair: Sounds good.

[22:44] Sean Gallagher: Can we talk briefly about container runtime differences? We use containerd. Does it matter?

[22:51] Alex Chen: Usually not directly, but kernel version and cgroup settings can. Also, make sure you’re not hitting GPU page faults due to memory oversubscription. But for inference, it’s mostly straightforward.

[23:07] Omar El-Sayed: We’ve seen occasional CPU steal time on shared nodes.

[23:11] Miguel Ortega: That will absolutely show up in streaming metrics. So again: dedicated nodes.

[23:18] Sean Gallagher: Agreed.

[23:20] Rina Kobayashi: We also do network streaming; client reads can cause backpressure. We’re trying to measure server push not client bottleneck.

[23:28] Alex Chen: Keep load gen on the same network fabric, and use a client that can keep up. Otherwise you’re benchmarking your TCP stack.

[23:39] Rina Kobayashi: (laughs) yep.

[23:41] Sana Farid: For run manifests, do you recommend recording network path info?

[23:47] Miguel Ortega: If it’s easy—like region, AZ, whether it’s same VPC. But don’t overdo it.

[23:56] Hiro Tanaka: Okay.

[24:00] (brief crosstalk)

[24:02] Priya Nair: One more: for driver versions, are you planning to standardize on one per quarter?

[24:08] Hiro Tanaka: Yes. We’re freezing a Q1 2026 baseline anchor build. We want the environment frozen too.

[24:15] Alex Chen: Great. Just be cautious: security patches sometimes require driver updates. But if you must update, treat it as a new baseline.

[24:27] Sean Gallagher: That’s a good policy.

[24:30] Rina Kobayashi: For DCGM, can you send recommended sampling config that doesn’t add overhead?

[24:36] Alex Chen: Yes. We’ll send a note: sample at 1s or 5s, don’t do super high frequency. And capture summary stats plus raw time series.

[24:48] Rina Kobayashi: Okay.

[24:50] Hiro Tanaka: I think we’ve covered it. Let’s do recap + next steps.

[24:55] Hiro Tanaka: Redwood action items: Rina will add nvidia-smi/DCGM capture to harness artifacts. Sean updates the bench cluster runbook with persistence, exclusivity, and CPU pinning. Sana writes warmup and measurement window policy for noise model. I’ll send our driver/CUDA/Triton matrix to NVIDIA.

[25:17] Alex Chen: And NVIDIA side: we’ll send recommended clock/power guidance per SKU and a short set of commands you can paste into runbooks.

[25:27] Priya Nair: Also we’ll propose a short follow-up after you do a controlled rerun.

[25:33] Sean Gallagher: Can we target next week? Maybe 30 minutes.

[25:36] Priya Nair: Yep.

[25:38] Hiro Tanaka: Great. Anything else before we drop?

[25:42] Omar El-Sayed: All good.

[25:44] Sana Farid: Thanks everyone.

[25:46] Alex Chen: Thanks.

[25:47] Priya Nair: Thanks.

---

Auto-generated notes (Fireflies):
